'''Michel C. Nussenzweig''' (born 10 February 1955) is a professor and head of the Laboratory of Molecular Immunology at [[The Rockefeller University]] and a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] investigator. He is a member of both the US [[National Academy of Medicine]] and the [[US National Academy of Sciences]].

==Education and career==
Nussenzweig graduated summa cum laude with a B.A. degree from New York University College of Arts and Sciences in 1975. He earned a Ph.D. from The Rockefeller University in 1981 in cellular immunology, working in [[Zanvil A. Cohn]]’s laboratory with [[Ralph M. Steinman]] on groundbreaking studies of mouse dendritic cells.

As a Ph.D. student, Nussenzweig was the first to show that dendritic cells present foreign antigens to initiate T cell immunity.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nussenzweig|first1=M. C.|last2=Steinman|first2=R. M.|title=Contribution of dendritic cells to stimulation of the murine syngeneic mixed leukocyte reaction|journal=The Journal of Experimental Medicine|date=1 May 1980|volume=151|issue=5|pages=1196–1212|doi=10.1084/jem.151.5.1196|pmid=6445399|language=en|issn=0022-1007|pmc=2185855}}</ref> He also produced the first dendritic cell-specific [[monoclonal antibody]] and cloned the first dendritic cell receptor.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nussenzweig|first1=M C|last2=Steinman|first2=R M|last3=Witmer|first3=M D|last4=Gutchinov|first4=B|title=A monoclonal antibody specific for mouse dendritic cells|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|date=1 January 1982|volume=79|issue=1|pages=161–165|pmc=345682|issn=0027-8424|bibcode=1982PNAS...79..161N|pmid=6948298|doi=10.1073/pnas.79.1.161|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Nussenzweig received an M.D. from New York University School of Medicine in 1982 and completed his internship and residency in internal medicine, and a clinical fellowship in infectious diseases at [[Massachusetts General Hospital]] in 1985. From 1986 to 1989, he was a postdoctoral fellow in genetics in the Harvard Medical School laboratory of [[Philip Leder]]. Nussenzweig returned to The Rockefeller University as an assistant professor in 1990 and he became an associate professor in 1994, and a professor and senior physician in 1996. In 2013, he was named the first Zanvil A. Cohn and Ralph M. Steinman Professor.<ref>{{cite web|title=Heads of Laboratory: Michel C. Nussenzweig|url=http://www.rockefeller.edu/research/faculty/labheads/MichelNussenzweig/#content|website=The Rockefeller University|accessdate=16 Aug 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Immunity and Tolerance|url=http://www.hhmi.org/research/immunity-and-tolerance|website=Howard Hughes Medical Institute|accessdate=16 Aug 2016}}</ref>

==Summary of research achievements==
Nussenzweig studies molecular aspects of the immune system’s adaptive and innate responses, using a combination of biochemistry, molecular biology, and genetics. Work on adaptive immunity focuses on B lymphocytes and antibodies to HIV-1, while work on innate immunity focuses on dendritic cells.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Scheid|first1=Johannes F.|last2=Mouquet|first2=Hugo|last3=Feldhahn|first3=Niklas|last4=Seaman|first4=Michael S.|last5=Velinzon|first5=Klara|last6=Pietzsch|first6=John|last7=Ott|first7=Rene G.|last8=Anthony|first8=Robert M.|last9=Zebroski|first9=Henry|last10=Hurley|first10=Arlene|last11=Phogat|first11=Adhuna|last12=Chakrabarti|first12=Bimal|last13=Li|first13=Yuxing|last14=Connors|first14=Mark|last15=Pereyra|first15=Florencia|last16=Walker|first16=Bruce D.|last17=Wardemann|first17=Hedda|last18=Ho|first18=David|last19=Wyatt|first19=Richard T.|author20-link=John R. Mascola|last20=Mascola|first20=John R.|last21=Ravetch|first21=Jeffrey V.|last22=Nussenzweig|first22=Michel C.|title=Broad diversity of neutralizing antibodies isolated from memory B cells in HIV-infected individuals|journal=Nature|date=2 April 2009|volume=458|issue=7238|pages=636–640|doi=10.1038/nature07930|pmid=19287373|bibcode=2009Natur.458..636S|s2cid=4399760}}</ref> The laboratory has isolated and cloned human antibodies to HIV-1 and explored their roles in prevention and therapy. In clinical trials, a broadly neutralizing antibody isolated from an HIV-infected patient was shown to be safe and effective and to interfere with chronic infection in a way that traditional antiretroviral therapy does not.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Halper-Stromberg|first1=Ariel|last2=Lu|first2=Ching-Lan|last3=Klein|first3=Florian|last4=Horwitz|first4=Joshua
